If I could somehow send the 22 year old version of me all of the Mr. Money Mustache Classics articles I would, and I still re-read them on a regular basis to help build my “frugality muscle”. No, I don’t need that silly trinket, just like MMM skipped buying the drinking flask. Yes, there is great joy to be had by giving yourself a haircut or making a low cost homemade pizza or taking a brisk walk outside on a very cold, dark night and marveling at stars and planets (all referenced in various MMM articles).

Regardless of how high house prices are, or how much money you make, I believe there is great value in practicing Mustachianism. Thank you, MMM, for writing them – keep ’em’ coming!

I agree I’ve always been surprised how move averse people are. I thought remote work would change that much more than it has.

It’s *not* easy at all to make new friends as an adult. We moved after FI’ing in our 30s and still don’t have a friend group as strong as the one we left behind a few years ago.

But also what strikes me is the persistent assumption that everyone needs to own a house. I’ve never owned a house and never even lived in one as an adult. I do own a boat however, which is like a tiny house, that we’ve lived on for 7 years. Renting a small apartment is perfectly valid.

I would suggest to your commenter that he explore the “tiny house/dwelling” movement. Changing the size of your home is often an even easier way to save than location arbitrage. Humans don’t need really need as much space as they think (many average suburban homes feel “mansion-sized” to me).

For example, in my 20s I lived in an 800 sq ft nice apartment and then switched to a 350 sq ft (!!!) studio in a less nice building for a few years, and saved a ton that way.

Totally agree on the not needing as much space as you think. Five years ago I got rid of the last of my things and moved into my (very) minimalist campervan. Five years ago! I must say, houses are so inefficient with their layout, their size, and the way cities are designed around them (almost necessitating cars) that I don’t think I’ll ever own one. I simply can not endorse a design that isolates people from each other making everyone miserable, while at the same time dramatically increasing the cost of living and pollution. I guess I’m weird but I have never cared much about having friends. Between family, work, and hobbies, I’m covered. Now if a hobby or interest introduces me to someone interesting I’m open to it but otherwise I’m too busy to just “hang out” with people anymore.

I recently bought my first home using the little known hack called “marry an electrician and then get a house with all knob and tube wiring, because no one else will want it due to the wires being old, even though if they were going to burn the house down they likely would have by now.”

Seems to be going very well thus far, and there is a bus at the end of my street which I can take to the city center in 15 minutes for $2.

(I will specify that I did not marry the electrician solely because of their career. They have other qualities.)

Yup. Homes that need remodeling and new plumbing or electrical can be had for hundreds of thousands less in hotter markets. Having the trade or skills to do the work will save so much money.

I’ve added probably between $20k and $75k in value to each of my homes in these ways–always spending way less than the value returned by either doing most of the work myself or contracting out after many bids and significant time considering the design. I’ve never had a house sit on the market. All have gone under contract at about ask or over in a few days or less.

Today my FIRE life consists of travelling between Cairns & Niigata 10 months of the year and the remaining 2 months somewhere else in the world.

The cost? Holding cost of Cairns & Niigata apartments are total approx $10k USD pa. Another $5k USD for travel/flights/shinkansen etc, $15k USD pa more for day to day living expenses and another $10k USD pa for fun (Fat FIRE).

My point is and hopefully it also inspires others I’m living comfortably on $40k USD pa, living in two countries, and travelling to other countries too (in March I’m heading to Malaysia, Thailand and Philippines for 8 weeks), this tick all my boxes (nature, beaches, mountains, intellectual stimulation, cuisine, friendships and new adventures).

Can I afford to be spending more on my current lifestyle? Heck yes. This current lifestyle spending is actually less than 20% pa of my annual investment income. So why didn’t I do all this earlier?

As to high incomes, yes our clients valued our services and paid us well, however in truth money was/has never been never been my main driver, it was just the result of putting others (our clients) first. What I’ve appreciated about the Moustachian philosophy (at least from what I can tell) is that it doesn’t assume that we humans deserve to get everything we want and right now!

I’m actually a compulsive debtor in recovery, and reading blogs like this one and books like “Your Money or Your Life,” are very helpful tools for me. My past ridiculous and childish thoughts about money included:

~I deserve this ~Everyone else is doing it, I should be able to as well ~It’s my right ~I shouldn’t have to work and save. I shouldn’t have to sacrifice or make difficult choices.

These thoughts and the silly and financially damaging actions they lead to are not just the affliction of those who are compulsive, but are the foundational philosophy for our consumerist culture.

Just because I live in the U.S., doesn’t mean I deserve to be able to buy a house; especially when I did NOTHING during my pre-recovery days to save for one.

The amazing news is, however, that even though I got into recovery and began to practice sound financial principles only 10 years ago, my hubs and I own a great home in a dream location. We went from overspending each month by about $1,500 (today we’d be almost $250,000 in debt – and that doesn’t include interest payments!) to being worth over $1.5 million (this does include the estimated value of our home).

I work in my dream career and make 2/3 as much money as my hubby, but work 1/4 the time he does (this is the way we both like it).

All this to say that once you turn the ship around, once you begin to change even the smallest behaviors with money to align with Moustachian ideas, it doesn’t take long at all to see HUGE results.

Thanks, Mr. Moustache and all who embrace FIRE and principles of financial sanity! Natalie :^)

I did end up moving and found a whole new and better life!

I had been ‘living’ in San Francisco as a flight attendant in a 3 bedroom with 18 roommates for $375/mo. Since the crew is never there, it wasn’t as uncomfortable but it is the only way that situation worked for the 3 years I did it. I saved a bunch of money and paid off my debts. It also helped socially because our schedules were so wild it was the best way to spend time with people. If I had a bunch of days home I would visit family or friends. My parents were kind enough to store my few items in a spare closet of their house.

I had begun making an excel of places I thought I would like to live and move to then the pandemic hit and it forced me to move as I was laid off. I made a list of requirements including drivable in 2 hours to a major airport/hub or closer if I commuted (I don’t have to go to work every day). It needed to be affordable housing, community-based, good internet (my parents live in Alabama and it’s not available where they live), things for me to do (entertainment), and in a climate with 4 seasons (Alabama has hot or wet, SFO has damp and less damp). I used best places which has a quiz that also asked some other good questions and I decided I probably wanted some kind of university town so there was 24 hour services (because sometimes I work nights) as that would be good for me. I then converted my Honda crv to a van and road tripped and stayed a few days to a week in each area I was considering. When I got to my current town of Harrisonburg Va I fell in love with it. I moved there and bought a house within a few months for $1,100 a month. It needs work since it was built in 1918 but I enjoy that and it has great bones. I put in my transfer to IAD and love it. I later was able to go to a meet up for board gamers which is one of my favorite hobbies. I made a lot of friends and met my husband. Now that I’m back to flying I find I enjoy being home more because I’m not stressed about money since I moved someplace more reasonable and built myself a whole new community for support.

Just move and put yourself out there. Most people are too lazy to make new friends, it takes work and practice but it’s not impossible to make yourself a a new home.

That is so weird. We drove around and spent the night there. It was a great surprise! Virginia really wasn’t on the list., but we were really struck how nice it is.As I mentioned in another post, Fayetteville, Arkansas was also a pleasant surprise. Missouri seemed to have the nicest people. The skid plate under our car was badly damaged when I drove over something and many people stopped and offered to help.

In his book, Paul Terhorst suggested retiring to a State capitol that has a major university,.

I work part time in retail, my wife part time at a library. I found your blog and read every article from beginning to end. We bought a house and have no other debt and currently about 40k invested, not counting our retirement accounts through work, and it started here. I constantly hear comments like the one quoted and continuously have people that make way more than me question how I afford my life. I point them here and know they’re too lazy and married to their excuses they won’t even bother. Everyone loves to complain these days.

I think it’s worth pointing out that “house hacking” does not necessitate breaking your home up into multiple ADUs in the US as you have highlighted through many follower stories on your blog. That being said I hope the broader point you’ve been making since the start of the pandemic will resonate with folks – these swings are long cycles and there are mustachaian activities to participate in even when real estate is off the table. I’m only able to consider moving to the CO area this year after much thumb twiddling in far more affordable Nebraska!

Love this! While I do feel super lucky to have bought my place in Longmont pre-pandemic, after a few years I realized it wasn’t where I wanted to be anymore. I was tired of winter, tired of grind culture, and ready for a big adventure. I spent a year traveling in Latin America, lowkey looking for a new country to live in, and I ended up loving Colombia. Incredible natural beauty, tons to explore, nice people, and an excellent exchange rate. Currently renting a 1BR apartment in a small, safe, outdoorsy city for $260/mo. Hope you’re enjoying winter in AZ, the community you joined sounds awesome!

Thank you Pete. 8 years ago, we decided to relocate from Massachusetts to Tucson, AZ. The transition came with many challenges, but we have never looked back and are really grateful that we made this choice. We have experienced many benefits, including lower cost of living, sunnier weather, more access to nature, better shopping options, meeting new friends, and more. This is a great article that challenges all of us to take action instead of feeling like the world is against us.

Imagine my surprise, when scrolling down through the article to see my hometown of fort Madison, Iowa listed near the top of the affordable cities list! 15,000 people. I will say this, there is a reason why the cost is under $100 per square foot: Good paying jobs are scarce, amenities are non-existent, the schools are mediocre at best. Do yourself a favor, don’t save $50,000 on housing to sacrifice far more than that in future earnings. I can’t comment on overall life satisfaction, because, to each their own… It is a somewhat charming riverside city, but please, spend the money to live in a more desirable location. Strike a better balance.

Howdy fellow Iowan! Funny to read this as one of my friends just relocated to Fort Madison, IA because of the cheaper housing costs compared to the big city of Cedar Rapids :) where he was living. Of course Cedar Rapids, IA is still way way way cheaper than the East Coast where I moved from in 2015 for my own geographical arbitrage, in no small part because of this blog. But my friend found a good job before he moved to Fort Madison which is key, (he’s an electrician), even cheaper housing than Cedar, and so far is good with the move and likes Fort Madison – exactly your point about to each his own and it being a charming riverside city on the Mississippi.

Nice read. I myself have done pretty well with a couple of those strategies: first geoarbitrage in Japan (although I speak the language), then house hacking. We could live for roughly $2k/mo. living downtown in a 2nd-tier Japanese city (Sendai). Safe, convenient, great food. On house hacking, I studied up for years on real estate so I get how that may be daunting to some, but for us it’s turned into living for free for 2 years, then more recently choosing to pay half the mortgage to help out family. It takes work, but it will pay off if you put in the effort.

To those who still think house hacking is too hard, there’s a simple solution that’s old as dirt: Get a roommate. Get two even. If owning eventually is part of your dream, put whatever you save in housing expenses into a down payment savings account and pull the trigger once ready. After all, house hacking is basically just buying a house and then getting a roommate(s). If you’re reading this, MMM has already given you the tools; the only one capable of stopping you is yourself.

Lastly, on cheaper markets I’d find livable, on the East Coast I like Baltimore. You definitely have to be careful where you buy, but there’s opportunity for sure. Philly is another great place as mentioned above. I wouldn’t go anywhere near Cumberland (on MMM’s $200k list), but Pittsburgh might also be worth a look.

Good article! I would add to the suggestions to look for towns/cities that have Greyhound and related bus access and ideally also Amtrak right now. Additionally, use tools such as realtor.com to look at some of the major environmental risks (flood and fire) of any property being considered; having environmental risk integrated with real estate search engines is a relatively new feature, and unfortunately some of the best “deals” are squarely in the path of danger, from my experience. Finally, check relocation places out in person — ideally arriving without a car (such as by Amtrak or Greyhound) to see how it goes for you.

We have just sold our house near Austin, TX and moved our family of 5 to Lafayette, CO. Cost of living is significantly higher here and houses are incredibly expensive. My spouse is transgender and did not feel safe in TX anymore; We had to go. How strange to be political refugees. I never could have imagined us in this position. Due to housing prices in our new city, we have decided to become renters as we continue to pursue FI. Our equity money is going into the market. It feels very odd and countercultural to make this decision, but here we are. After decades of homeownership, have we gone backwards? Or will we be better off? Time will tell.

Mr. Money Mustache February 5, 2024, 2:35 pm

Welcome new neighbor! Maybe we’ll see you at one of our events at the MMMHQ Coworking space just up the road in Longmont this spring.

We probably should move, not because housing is unaffordable, in fact a massive home is $200k. Due to currency depreciation a home bought for $200k in 2010 is now only $80k. So housing is cheaper, but is a function of a dysfunctional economy.

However, many friends have moved to other countries because of a weak economy over past 2 decades. But to move it means we need to leave family behind, especially older parents. It is very hard to leave behind family connections, so we stay.

I guess you just have to be happy with your choices, because everything is a choice.

As others have said, the first half of this article (the FRED graph of average sales prices across the US) is statistically questionable and has the feel of “see? housing is actually affordable, you’re just wrong to be looking at actual sales prices in your area”. As you mention, it’s a national average, when all RE markets are local, so it’s unclear what it means at all. Another distortion is that the FRED data comes from FHA, which means that it excludes cash sales and sales with jumbo loans. This distortion tends to result in lower home prices than you see when looking at, say, the Case-Schiller data. Even if you average over the whole country.

But I’m glad I ground through that part because the rest of this has some really practical advice for how to find somewhere to live. There is a classic old Raptitude post “Most Lives are Lived by Default” which suggests that probably your current location is a side-effect of your job, or school, or relationship, and that you could do better if you actively tried to find the “right” location for you. Unfortunately the article provides no advice for _how_ to do this; it mostly suggests moving to a different neighborhood in your current town, with the assumption that you have a good idea of whether you want to be closer/further to nightlife or grocery stores or bike paths or whatever, and you just need to pull the trigger.

But for somebody who is near-FIRE, or “FIRE except for housing”, it’s hard to figure out where to even start. These resources are a great way to filter for locations that are financially reasonable and also in the right part of the country. Another thing I did was keep an eye on r/financialindependence and r/fatfire to see if anybody posted cool understated places to live. Chattanouga popped up, as did Kansas City MO, and Asheville NC.

In 2020 I visited a pile of such cities, as well as big ones like Philly and Portland and NYC, by going on AirBNB and finding a spare room that I could rent for a month or more. In the Portland area I wound up doing this for several months in a row, since it’s a huge place and you can change locations dramatically without leaving the metro area.

When I first started doing this I would always look to stay in whole houses, but this is the wrong approach! Aside from not distorting housing markets by using SFHs as hotels, you actually want to find a place with a host who you can talk to about the city and who can tell you about different neighborhoods. And if you rent spare rooms for long periods, it’s a surprisingly affordable thing to do. Especially as you can often meet people who are willing to let you stay with them without going through a fee-skimming platform like AirBNB.

This strategy might only be practical for single light-travelling digital nomad types but I encourage anybody to seriously consider it.

Thanks for the Albuquerque shoutout! It’s not a perfect place to live, but if you like being outside, it’s hard to do better for what it costs to live here.

FIRE is often about making different choices than everyone else to emphasize the things that really matter to you. You rent a small apartment close to work instead of buying a McMansion in the exurbs. You bike or walk instead of driving a 3-row SUV. You cook at home instead of eating out. You go to the library instead of the movie theater…

…and you move to New Mexico instead of Colorado.

If you’re still working, the national labs are solidly above-average employers that emphasize work-life balance. The outdoor recreation is almost as good as Colorado, and Durango is only a few hours away if you want bigger mountains. There’s a nice airport, a zoo, great museums, and 3 Costcos. The weather is great: cooler than Phoenix in the summer, warmer than Denver in the winter, and sunny almost all the time. Plus, the state is doing lots to support working families, with subsidized daycare and free college tuition.

So if you’re discouraged about how much it costs to live in Bend or Boulder, make less popular choice and check out New Mexico.

As a former Coloradoan, newly adopted New Mexican I can reiterate Joel’s statements. NM isn’t perfect but I feel like I have greater access to outdoor recreation here in NM than I did in the Front Range of Colorado, plus much less people to compete with. There are slightly more sunny days, so I can’t complain about that either.

I’m in Santa Fe, which is pretty comparable to many parts of Colorado regarding cost of living and the weather feels nearly identical to Colorado with our almost 7000′ elevation. Santa Fe punches above it’s weight as a city in regards to culture, restaurants, and museums. There is a good bit of tourism that feeds into that, but the restaurant scene is pretty great. The history of the region keeps me engaged as I continue to learn more about the area.

I keep eyeballing the affordability of Albuquerque and the offerings of a city that is 5x the size of Santa Fe, but Santa Fe fits the bill for now

The key thing, as this article exemplifies, is to EXAMINE both reality, and your own assumptions. So much “can’t afford a house” mania is based on vague unexamined feelings, and vague media-based proclamations. When you cut through that with a bunch of facts and self-examination . . . the world opens up. As this piece shows. In our case, a limiting factor (we thought) was the “must be close to family” idea. Then we realized that 1. family members keep making plans and moving without consulting us, so why base our whole lives on their (temporary) locations? 2. once we did the math and realized how often we “see family” it became clear that 3 visits a year with a couple of family events each time would cover all the hanging-out time we do, anyway. YMMV.

We love to see these people! But in reality, they’re all busy, they move around, and there’s a limit to everyone’s time. So now we are free to live mostly in Europe, where we prefer to be (and where it’s cheap to live a great, low-footprint life), and not feel disloyal because of some presumed idea of “being too far away from family.” We see them as much as ever did! Now it’s just during our annual out-and-back migration. So yeah: really, truly examine everything that seems to be liming your choices.

I think the one thing you missed calling out is how this is especially relevant to FIRE folks who are no longer working. Many of these lower cost cities don’t have the high paying jobs that really helps us along the way.

Personally I went the route of moving to a small apartment and renting in a HCOL city to maximize my income in my younger years. Now that I’m coming up on 40, I’ve moved to a small town in MN and enjoying the much lower cost of living.

The other cool aspect of this idea is that you can live in a very neat neighborhood within these type of towns. For example, I’m living in the heart of the historic neighborhood within walking distance of two lakes and downtown for super cheap. If I had done that in any moderate cost of living city, I’d pay 5-10x as much for housing. So while it’s a small town, it’s still very walkable & bikeable because I’m not stuck out in some suburban wasteland.

#8766. This Year’s NYC Marathon Proved Different Strategies Can Lead to Victory

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

I’m sure I could think of a couple of thousand ways, many of which include espresso, to spend a Sunday morning in New York City than running 26.2 miles through all five boroughs. But on Nov. 1, nearly 60,000 people decided to run the New York City Marathon—again—like they have every year since 1970. Some were chasing a championship. Some were chasing a personal best. Others probably just wanted to finish before their feet decided to go on strike. And there are hosts of runners dressed in all kinds of costumes just out for a jog. And the crowd keeps everyone well cheered on. No matter who it is.

The men’s winner was Andreas Almgren of Sweden, who covered the course in two hours, six minutes, one second. And I’m going to put an asterisk next to it because this was his first marathon. Not his first race, obviously. Almgren arrived as the reigning world half-marathon champion and European 10,000-meter champion. He’d spent years developing the engine. He just hadn’t taken it out for this particular 26.2-mile test drive.

The lead pack stayed together deep into the race, and Almgren waited until the final mile to make his decisive move. Italy’s Yemaneberhan Crippa finished second, thirteen seconds behind him, and Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho was third. Defending champion Benson Kipruto wound up fourth. That’s quite a debut, particularly on a course that includes bridges, hills, crazy potholes and enough turns to get you lost.

Before anybody decides the lesson is to skip marathon preparation, understand what a debut means here. Almgren wasn’t some guy who woke up last Thursday and discovered running shoes. He had world-class credentials at shorter distances. Moving up required applying an already extraordinary aerobic foundation to a longer event. A marathon is not merely two half-marathons stapled together. Fueling, pacing, muscular endurance, and how you respond after mile twenty all become rather important when your body starts negotiating terms of surrender.

The women’s race was even more entertaining near the finish. Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui reclaimed the title she’d won in 2024, finishing in 2:24:36. Defending champion Hellen Obiri was in the fight late, but American Jess McClain came charging from behind and passed her in the closing meters. Chepkirui won, McClain took second in 2:24:42, and Obiri was third one second later. McClain became the first American woman on the New York podium since 2018.

And if you think the only interesting athletes are the ones with the smallest numbers on the clock, the wheelchair divisions cranks them out! Switzerland’s Marcel Hug won his eighth New York title in 1:28:14, edging American Daniel Romanchuk by one second. Catherine Debrunner, also Swiss, won the women’s wheelchair race in 1:40:02, nearly eight and a half minutes ahead of Tatyana McFadden. Same city, same event, completely different demands on the athlete. The upper-body power, equipment handling, and tactical judgment involved deserve more attention than they usually get.

Then there’s Mildred Baker, an 80-year-old Bronx resident who took up running in her late seventies and completed her first marathon in 7:03:49. Seven freakin’ hours! No, Almgren is not the only champion. That’s the point. The marathon can be a world championship-level knife fight at the front and a personal expedition at the back. And a trade in between. You can appreciate both extremes without pretending they’re the same athletic achievement.

Secondly, I must admit that l like the way this race exposes a certain kind of gym stupidity: the assumption that only one type of physical performance counts. A Swedish speed merchant conquered a distance he’d never raced. An American woman stole second place in the final strides. An 80-year-old finished something most people wouldn’t even start. You’re actually, in one Sunday event, looking at the entire definition of fitness.

#8763. Bodybuilder AJ Ellison Shares 3 tips for Fat Loss After 50

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

IFBB Pro and Masters Men’s Physique Competitor Adam J. Ellison may be 50 years old, but he has a physique that would make most men half his age green with envy. Fortunately, the proud father of three kids says that it is still possible to drop fat while juggling the responsibilities of work and family, as he shared his “No B.S. guide” on Instagram.

AJ Ellison knows that fat mass tends to increase while lean muscle decreases with age, and science suggests that the slow down in metabolic rates could play a significant role as to why it is harder to drop body fat as we age, but that doesn’t mean that we should ditch our physique goals  as we mature. Ellison, now 50 years old, is still winning competitions on stage, and looked phenomenal as he topped the Master’s 50+ Men’s Physique category at the 2026 IFBB Masters World Championships. He even placed second in the 40+, meaning that AJ is still hanging with those who are up to a decade younger than himself. With all that in mind, here are his tips for dropping stubborn fat.

“Fat loss doesn’t start in the gym, it starts in your kitchen,” wrote Ellison. “You can’t out-train a poor diet.” The big man also said that he makes sure to consume plenty of protein. “Aim for 50 to 70g of protein at every meal. Build every plate around protein first. Fill the rest with whole foods.”

“Most men try to burn more calories. That’s backwards,” said Ellison. “Protect your muscle first.” While muscle does not burn calories directly, the presence of more muscle tissue means that there is a greater level of energy required in the body, leading to a greater calorie requirement.

To build muscle, the competitive bodybuilder suggested that we “Lift 3 to 4 times every week,” and added that for hypertrophy, “Progress your lifts whenever possible.”

“Cardio is a tool. It isn’t the foundation,” believes Ellison, who utilizes cardiovascular training to support his efforts without making it the center of his ethos. “Strength training should always come first,” wrote the master, for his almost 900K Instagram followers.

To make sure that cardio is part of the mix, “Add 8,000 to 10,000 daily steps,” enthused Ellison. “Use cardio to support recovery, not to punish yourself.”

Summing up, the bodybuilder noted that “Small calorie deficits beat aggressive diets,” observing that “Crash dieting teaches your body to conserve energy.” So, to get started, Ellison coached that we should aim to lose 0.5 to 1% of body fat per week, and to trust in the process. “Track your progress for at least three weeks before changing anything,” he concluded.

The highest-value hotel redemption for families using Chase Ultimate Rewards

Picture this: your kids are splashing in an infinity pool that overlooks the turquoise Caribbean, your partner is sipping a cocktail at the swim-up bar, and you're on your third gourmet meal of the day — all without opening your wallet once. No mental math at dinner. No "should we do the excursion?" budget anxiety. Just a genuinely luxurious family vacation where everything is already paid for. This is what the Hyatt All-Inclusive sweet spot feels like. And the ChooseFI community has quietly been using it to take family vacations that their neighbors are financing on credit card debt — except you're doing it nearly free. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva property — think Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, or Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana — will typically run **$500 to $1,500 per night** in cash when you factor in the all-inclusive rate for two adults and two kids. Over a five-night stay, you're looking at a cash outlay of $2,500 to $7,500. That's a trip many families save years for. With World of Hyatt points, that same night costs **25,000 points**. At a cash rate of $1,000 per night (a very achievable number at peak Ziva properties), you're extracting **4 cents per point** in value — and at $1,500 per night, you're pushing **6 cents per point**. The industry benchmark for a "good" hotel redemption is 1-2 cents per point. You're doubling or tripling that benchmark on a family vacation. The pricing inefficiency here is structural and beautiful: Hyatt's award chart is **fixed**, meaning they set a category for each property based on its tier, not its cash price. All-inclusive resorts are priced in the award chart like any other Hyatt — but the cash rate includes *every meal, every drink, every activity*. The loyalty program hasn't fully "priced in" the all-inclusive premium. That gap is your opportunity. For families pursuing FI, this redemption is especially powerful because the value scales with family size. Four people eating and drinking all day at a resort adds up fast in cash — but costs exactly the same 25,000 points whether it's two people or a family of six. The bigger your family, the more you win.

The core insight here is understanding what the 25,000 points actually buys — and why Hyatt's award chart creates an accidental arbitrage for all-inclusive resorts.

World of Hyatt uses a fixed award chart, categorizing properties from Category 1 (3,500 points/night) to Category 8 (45,000 points/night). Hyatt Ziva and Hyatt Zilara properties typically fall in the Category 4–6 range (18,000–25,000 points/night depending on the specific property and season). The key word is fixed: your points cost doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash prices do. A sold-out week during spring break or Christmas holiday that drives cash rates to $1,500/night still costs the same 25,000 points as an off-peak Tuesday.

Now layer on the all-inclusive structure. When you book a Hyatt Ziva or Hyatt Zilara on points, all meals, drinks, and activities are included in the award rate. This isn't a separate fee. This isn't a resort charge tacked on. The award redemption covers the full all-inclusive experience — the same unlimited dining, premium open bar, water sports, and entertainment that cash guests pay for. Hyatt is one of the few hotel brands that doesn't strip out the all-inclusive component when you book with points.

The Transfer Path: Chase Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt

This is where the ChooseFI earning strategy snaps into place. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, instantly. There's no waiting period, no processing delay — you initiate the transfer and the points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, instantly, which matters if you're earning points on rent payments through the Bilt Mastercard.

The transfer ratio is significant because Chase UR points are among the easiest transferable points to earn in volume. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Chase Ink Business Preferred, and Chase Ink Business Cash/Unlimited (when paired with a Sapphire card) all feed into the same UR pool. A family spending across categories can accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually, which translates directly into four or more nights at a Ziva property.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges or carrier-imposed fees on award bookings. The only cost you'll pay out-of-pocket is the government taxes on your award night — typically $10–25 per night depending on the property location. Your 25,000 points buys you a clean, nearly free night without surprise fees draining the value.

Family vs. Adults-Only: Know Which Property to Book

Hyatt Ziva properties are family-friendly — kids are welcome, family suites are available, and there are dedicated kids' clubs and activities. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only. This distinction matters enormously when booking. Searching for availability and finding great dates at a Zilara won't help if you're bringing a 9-year-old. Always confirm the property type before transferring points.

Before searching for availability, confirm your points position. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards and check your combined UR balance across all eligible cards. Remember, points from Chase Ink cards can be pooled with your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred. You'll need at least 25,000 points per night you want to book — a five-night trip requires 125,000 points. If you're close but not there, set a target date 3–4 months out and focus earning in the meantime.

Go to hyatt.com and search for your target property directly. Use the "Use Points" toggle to see award availability. Key properties to search for families:

For adults-only trips, search Hyatt Zilara Cancun or Hyatt Zilara Cap Cana. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, so you can search nearly 13 months ahead — this is your best window for securing prime dates like school breaks, spring break, and holiday weeks.

Search flexible date ranges to find the best combination of availability and value. Hyatt's calendar view makes this efficient — you can see which nights have standard award availability vs. premium pricing. Note that some peak dates may show higher point requirements; always check if your target dates are at the standard 25,000-point rate or a peak rate.

Once you've confirmed award availability for your exact dates, navigate to Chase Ultimate Rewards and select "Transfer to Travel Partners." Choose World of Hyatt from the partner list. The transfer ratio is 1:1 and the transfer is instant — your Hyatt points will appear within minutes. Only transfer what you need for the specific booking; there's no reason to transfer excess points speculatively.

Return to hyatt.com, log into your World of Hyatt account, and complete the award booking for your confirmed dates. At checkout, select points as your payment method. You'll pay only minimal government taxes (typically $10–25/night). Keep your confirmation email — it will specify that the all-inclusive meals, beverages, and activities are included.

Award availability at popular Ziva/Zilara properties can be limited during peak school break windows. Your moves: (1) Search 395 days out as soon as your target dates open, (2) consider shoulder season dates that offer strong weather but lower demand, (3) call the World of Hyatt member line at 1-800-323-7249 — agents sometimes see availability the website doesn't display, (4) check alternate Ziva/Zilara properties in different destinations.

The math on Hyatt all-inclusive redemptions is what makes this a true sweet spot for the FI community. At a standard hotel, your points cover the room — but you still pay cash for meals, drinks, and activities. At an all-inclusive, the points rate covers everything: room, all meals, unlimited drinks, pool and beach access, kids clubs, entertainment, and most resort activities. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva paying $700 per night in cash (a common rate) would spend $4,900 for a 7-night stay — plus tips. The same stay at 25,000 points per night costs 175,000 World of Hyatt points total, which equals approximately $3,500 in transferable points value at a conservative 2 cents per point. But the actual value received is closer to $5,000 to $7,000 when you factor in all the meals, drinks, and activities that would cost extra at a regular hotel. This is why Hyatt all-inclusives consistently deliver 3 to 4 cents per point — double the already-strong Hyatt average.

Let's walk through a real family booking so you can see exactly how the numbers work.

The Trip: 5 Nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun for a Family of Four

You're planning a spring break trip — mid-April, when the weather in Cancun is spectacular and school is out. A family of four (two adults, two kids) wants five nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, one of the flagship all-inclusive properties in Hyatt's portfolio. This is a beachfront resort with multiple restaurants, a waterpark-style pool complex, and dedicated kids' programming.

The Cash Price: During spring break, Hyatt Ziva Cancun's all-inclusive rate for a family room runs approximately $900–$1,200 per night for a standard room, all meals and drinks included. At $1,000/night average, five nights costs $5,000 cash. At $1,200/night, you're at $6,000. That's real money for a family.

The Points Cost: At 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night, five nights costs 125,000 points. You'll pay approximately $75–100 total in government taxes across the stay. That's it.

The CPP Math: $5,000 value ÷ 125,000 points = 4 cents per point. At the higher cash rate of $6,000, you're at 4.8 cents per point. The World of Hyatt program's own editorial value benchmark is considered strong at 1.7 cents per point — you're earning nearly 3x that benchmark on this booking.

What Your Family Actually Gets: Every breakfast, lunch, and dinner at the resort's full-service restaurants. Unlimited alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages from morning coffee to late-night cocktails. The resort's pool complex with water slides the kids will talk about for years. Non-motorized water sports. Evening entertainment. This isn't a stripped-down experience — Hyatt Ziva is an upper-upscale brand, and the quality of food and service reflects it.

The Transfer: You move 125,000 Chase UR points to World of Hyatt at 1:1 — instantly — and book directly on hyatt.com. The entire booking process takes under 30 minutes once you have availability confirmed.

Book at the 395-Day Window for Peak Dates

Hyatt opens its booking window 395 days in advance — that's about 13 months. For spring break, Christmas week, and Thanksgiving, set a calendar reminder and search the moment your target dates become available. Families who wait until 6 months out regularly find those prime weeks already gone on points. This is the single biggest mistake families make with this redemption.

Search Multiple Properties to Triangulate Availability

Don't anchor on one property. Run searches simultaneously at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, and Hyatt Ziva Rose Hall. Different properties have different award release patterns, and finding five consecutive nights at one property is easier than it sounds if you're flexible about which destination.

Use 5th Night Free to Stretch Your Points Further

World of Hyatt has a 5th night free on award stays benefit for World of Hyatt credit card holders. Book five nights and pay points for only four. On a 5-night Ziva trip, that saves 25,000 points — enough for one additional night. If you have or are considering the World of Hyatt Credit Card, this benefit alone justifies it for this specific redemption.

The fastest path to 125,000 points for a 5-night family trip is the Chase trifecta: Sapphire Preferred or Reserve (dining and travel), Ink Business Preferred (business spending at 3x), and Ink Business Unlimited or Cash (flat-rate earning). A family running normal spending through these cards can realistically accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually.

This sounds obvious, but adults-only Zilara properties appear in the same search results as family-friendly Ziva properties. Always confirm the property type before transferring points. Once points are transferred into Hyatt, they don't transfer back to Chase.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with a small earning or redemption every two years. A single qualifying activity — even earning 1 point through a partner — resets the clock.

Avoid Booking Refundable Rates on Points Speculatively

Some members book award stays far out with the intent to cancel, just to "hold" dates. While Hyatt does allow cancellations, this practice can strain award availability for other members and creates unnecessary complexity. Book when you're confident.

This redemption was designed — structurally, if not intentionally — for families pursuing financial independence. Here's why it fits the ChooseFI worldview so perfectly.

The ideal user is a family of three to six people who want a high-quality, genuinely relaxing vacation without the mental overhead of per-meal, per-drink, per-activity budgeting. The all-inclusive format eliminates the "should we splurge on dinner?" anxiety that can undercut vacation enjoyment. You've already "paid" with points. Just enjoy.

You need a minimum of 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night. For a realistic 5-night family trip, plan for 125,000 points — or 100,000 if you hold the World of Hyatt card and qualify for the 5th night free benefit. This is very achievable if you've been accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards through normal household spending on a Sapphire card.

This redemption is also excellent for couples celebrating anniversaries or honeymoons (use Zilara for the adults-only experience), parents of young children who want a vacation where the kids are engaged so the adults can actually relax, and travelers who want a warm-weather, beach vacation without the complexity of international award flight bookings.

This is NOT the right fit if you prefer boutique, off-the-beaten-path travel over resort-style vacations, you're a solo traveler (the per-person value scales poorly), or you're chasing ultra-premium redemptions like business class flights or city luxury hotels. The Hyatt portfolio has those too — but this specific sweet spot is about maximum family value, not maximum luxury status.

This redemption earns an **Easy** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. The ChooseFI community members who struggle with it usually hit one of two friction points, and both are easily solved. **The Earning Side: Very Easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers 1:1 to World of Hyatt instantly. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you already have access to the best transfer path. Earning 125,000 Chase UR points for a 5-night trip is a reasonable 12–18 month project for a household running normal expenses through rewards cards. **The Booking Side: Easy, With One Catch.** The Hyatt website is clean and the points booking process is straightforward. The one challenge is **peak date availability** — spring break and holiday weeks book up fast at the most popular Ziva properties. The fix is simple: use the 395-day booking window. Set a phone reminder 13 months before your target trip and search the day availability opens. **The Transfer Confidence Hurdle.** Some beginners are nervous about transferring points to Hyatt before they have a confirmed booking. The practical risk is real — if you transfer and then can't find availability, those points are stranded in Hyatt (though they're still useful for future bookings). The solution: always **confirm availability before transferring**. Hyatt lets you select dates and see the points cost before you're asked to pay. Get to that confirmation screen first, then transfer. If you can navigate a hotel booking website and move money between financial accounts, you can execute this redemption. Start with a low-stakes search on hyatt.com today — just to get comfortable with how award availability looks.

Log into your World of Hyatt account and search for all-inclusive properties at your desired destination. Filter by the Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) or Hyatt Zilara (adults-only) brands. Check the nightly points rate — it will show the standard award rate and whether peak or off-peak pricing applies.

Check the same dates at the cash rate to calculate your cents per point value. If the cash rate is $600 per night and the award rate is 25,000 points, you are getting 2.4 cents per point. For all-inclusives, values above 2 cents per point are common and 3 or more cents per point is typical during peak season.

Transfer the required points from your Chase account to World of Hyatt. Transfers are instant. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, you can transfer directly. Freedom and Ink Cash points can be pooled to a Sapphire card first.

Complete the booking using your World of Hyatt points. Select the standard room type on points — all-inclusive benefits apply to all room categories. Add any special requests for your family (crib, connecting rooms, dietary needs) in the booking notes.

If you have World of Hyatt Globalist status (earned at 60 nights or through the Globalist challenge), you unlock suite upgrades (subject to availability), late checkout, and other premium benefits. Even without elite status, the all-inclusive base experience is exceptional — every meal, drink, and activity is covered.

A 7-night stay at a Hyatt Ziva or Zilara typically costs 175,000 to 245,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 to 35,000 per night depending on the property and season). This covers the room, all meals, unlimited drinks, activities, and entertainment for the duration of your stay.

At Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) properties, children typically stay and eat free when sharing a room with parents. Policies vary by property and the child's age — generally children under 12 are included at no additional cost. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only (18+). Check the specific property's policy when booking.

You can, but you will get significantly less value. The Chase portal values points at 1.25 cents (CSP) or 1.5 cents (CSR) per point. Transferring to Hyatt for an all-inclusive typically delivers 2 to 4 cents per point — roughly double the portal value. For a $600-per-night all-inclusive, the portal would cost 40,000 to 48,000 Chase points per night, while a direct Hyatt transfer costs only 25,000 points.

Most Hyatt all-inclusive award stays include resort fees in the points rate, but you may owe taxes and some incidental charges. Expect to pay $30 to $80 per night in local taxes depending on the country. Some premium experiences (spa treatments, excursions, premium alcohol) may carry additional charges. Tips for staff are at your discretion and appreciated.

Hyatt all-inclusive resorts represent the single best hotel redemption for families in the travel rewards ecosystem. The combination of a premium resort experience, all meals and drinks included, and 2 to 4 cents per point value makes this a sweet spot that is hard to beat. A family of four can enjoy a week-long beach vacation at a Hyatt Ziva for 175,000 transferable Chase points — a stay that would cost $4,000 to $7,000 in cash. For the ChooseFI community, this is the redemption that makes points tangible: your kids are splashing in the pool, you are enjoying a beachfront dinner, and the entire experience was covered by your Chase credit card rewards. Transfer to Hyatt, book early for peak dates, and give your family the vacation you have been optimizing for.

#8757. Stephan James Cut Weight in Order to Look Bigger for ‘I Play Rocky’

Stephan James is no stranger to playing a real-life person on screen. The award-winning actor put his best foot forward as Olympic running legend, Jesse Owens, in Race so he understands the importance of getting in shape for athletic roles. But to play the late, great Carl Weathers in I Play Rocky, the star tells M&F that he actually cut weight in order to look like his far larger hero.

Carl Weathers was in the NFL before his big break in the movies, but once the former Oakland Raider was cast as boxing champ Apollo Creed in the original Rocky, not to mention three successful sequels, it became clear that the star could blend his physicality as an athlete with the charisma required for the big screen.

At 6’2’’ and topping the scales at around 220 muscular pounds, Weathers frame is a difficult one to replicate. “So, that was my first thought: I had to put on a lot of weight, gotta put on a lot of muscle,” says James. “I was just over 200 pounds when I found out that I was going to play him in this film. And, speaking to one of my trainers, I was telling him about this plan to just start packing on all this weight and trying to turn it into muscle. And, he was like, ‘You know what, Steph? If you just try to cut your bodyfat percentage down, then you may give yourself a better chance, giving the perspective of somebody who is even bigger than you may actually be.’”

The tactic was a savvy one. Competitive bodybuilders have long known that decreasing levels of body fat makes for a more muscular looking physique. As fat stores shrink, the skin appears tighter against the muscle, making the most of those angles, edges, and separations that create definition. And, as the waistline decreases, the upper body appears wider, making the shoulders, chest, and arms look wider.

“I was able to cut down to about 180,” shares James, who continued to train for his fighting scenes while on a calorie deficit. “It really helped just emphasize and accentuate, you know, the muscles that I had. So, I was proud of what was the end result in the film.”

The Canadian actor says that he had just two months to get in shape to play Weathers, who passed away in 2024, and was hailed as Sylvester Stallone’s favorite onscreen opponent. James tells M&F that while he was previously “not big on cardio” before gaining the role, he soon understood that the iconic boxing battles between Creed and “The Italian Stallion” would force him to embrace the grind.

“I had to get very big on it during the process of making this film,” explains James, noting that mornings would consist of a cardio and weight training session, followed by learning the craft of boxing in the afternoons. “There was so much that I didn’t know and understand,” he recalls of stepping between the ropes. “From the footwork, to the technical, punches, then starting to learn the choreography. Cardio is the number one thing that you get from boxing. So, I think all of these things helped me cut the weight really fast, helping me to shred really, really, quickly.” The hard work certainly paid off, as Rocky fans have been quick to praise the casting of I Play Rocky, the story of how Sylvester Stallone defied the odds: writing and starring in one of the biggest movies of all time.

While Anthony Ippolito has Sly’s voice and body language down to a fine art, there’s more than a passing resemblance between Stephan James and Carl Weathers. The actor, who alongside brother Shamier Anderson, champions the representation of black talent with their nonprofit, The Black Academy, explains that he has a great deal of respect for the doors that Carl Weathers opened up for future generations. “Guys like Carl helped pave the way,” he tells M&F. “For so many other actors, like myself, to be able to be a leading man, to be seen as layered, characters with heart, thoughts, emotions, charisma and charm. Even his comedic beats. It’s not lost on me what Carl meant for that time, just being a pioneer.”

I Play Rocky hits theaters in the U.S. from Nov. 20.

Insights on building wealth, making informed career decisions, and achieving financial independence from a fellow physician.

Physician on FIRE and The Prudent Plastic Surgeon share a mission to help physicians build financial knowledge, independence, and control over their future.

Dr. Jordan Frey is a full-time practicing plastic surgeon and founder of The Prudent Plastic Surgeon, read by 20,000+ physicians. For five years, he has shared insights on personal finance, investing, career decisions, and financial independence while continuing to practice medicine.

A Physician on FIRE Partnership As part of our partnership, Physician on FIRE periodically shares select articles from The Prudent Plastic Surgeon with its readers.

About three months ago, I decided to actually give physician expert witness work a shot.

It was something that had been on my radar for a while. I knew other physicians did it. I knew it could be a lucrative side gig. And, at least on paper, it seemed to check a lot of the boxes that I look for in a physician side gig.

And three months later, after a bunch of cold outreach, a lot of conversations, a course on expert witness work, and several actual cases, including one involving a zebra, I figured it was a good time to share what I’ve learned so far.

The first thing I learned is that getting started in expert witness work is not particularly exciting.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

There was no moment where I signed up somewhere and cases suddenly started pouring in. Instead, there were a lot of emails, Zoom calls, and phone calls.

I reached out to lawyers. I talked to physicians who were already doing expert witness work. Plus I joined physician expert witness networks. I introduced myself, explained my expertise as a reconstructive plastic surgeon, sent my CV, and basically said, “If you ever need someone like me, keep me in mind.”

And I’ll admit, this felt a little uncomfortable. We aren’t really trained to market ourselves. For me, there was definitely a little bit of a feeling that I was shamelessly promoting myself. But eventually I started thinking about it differently.

We really are experts in our fields. And there are legal cases where an objective medical opinion can legitimately help a patient, a physician, or both. My job isn’t to advocate for whichever attorney happens to hire me. It’s to review the information and give an honest opinion based on my training and experience.

Once I reframed it that way, the outreach became a lot easier.

At the same time, I quickly realized that being an expert physician doesn’t automatically make you an expert witness. I understood the broad strokes. Review the medical records. Understand what happened. Form an opinion. Explain it.

But I didn’t really know how to structure a case review, what attorneys were looking for, how to write a report, how to create a fee schedule, or even how the business side of expert witness work typically operates.

That’s when I took Amy Fogelman’s High Rock Academy expert witness course. I found it incredibly helpful, particularly because it wasn’t just theoretical. There were actual resources and templates that I could use when cases started coming in, including report templates that I ultimately used for my first cases.

That preparation ended up being pretty well timed.

About six weeks after I really started pursuing this, I got my first case.

Ironically, my first case didn’t come from any of the cold outreach I had been doing. It came from a local physician friend who knew an attorney looking for someone with my expertise.

There’s probably an important lesson in there. You can send emails and join directories and market yourself all you want, but relationships still matter. The case involved aesthetic breast surgery and, to this point, has also been my most extensive case. There were a lot of records. There were depositions. And there were hours spent reviewing everything and figuring out exactly what happened.

Then I got on the phone with the attorneys.

This was probably the first time the work really clicked for me. They had very specific questions, and my job was essentially to do something that I already do every day as a physician: take a lot of complicated medical information, figure out what actually matters, form an opinion, and explain that opinion clearly.

That case is actually still ongoing, so there may be more work to come.

But after that first case, others started showing up.

I’ve now reviewed a handful of cases. Some have been relatively run-of-the-mill. And then there was the case involving an injury from a zebra.

I don’t remember that particular scenario coming up during plastic surgery residency.

But even that case reinforced what I’ve come to think is the biggest advantage of expert witness work for physicians: we already know how to do most of this. We spend our careers reviewing information, identifying what is relevant, synthesizing it, forming an assessment, and communicating that assessment to someone else. Sometimes that someone is a patient. Sometimes it’s another physician. And sometimes it’s an insurance company or hospital administrator.

In expert witness work, it happens to be an attorney.

That’s why, after only three months, I think this may be one of the better physician side gigs available. I used to list expert witness work as something I hadn’t personally done yet. Now I can at least start filling in that blank from experience.

Obviously, the income is part of the appeal.

One of the harder things when I started was figuring out what to charge. Talking to physicians who had done this before helped, as did seeing how others structured their fees.

I ultimately landed at $750 per hour with a five-hour minimum retainer.

So when I’m retained, I receive payment upfront for those first five hours. If the work goes beyond that, I bill additional time. I’ve had cases that exceeded the retainer and others that didn’t. But what matters to me isn’t just the hourly rate.

I’ve reviewed records early in the morning before my kids wake up. I’ve done work during their practices. And I’ve worked on cases in between operations while waiting for turnover.

That’s a meaningful distinction from clinical medicine, where income is about as directly tied to our physical presence as you can get. If I’m operating, seeing patients, or taking call, I can make money. If I’m not there, I generally don’t.

Expert witness work is still active income. I’m certainly not going to put it in the same category as the passive income streams I’ve built. But it’s active income on my terms.

Not every potential case turns into actual work.

This is particularly true with expert witness directories and referral companies. You may get contacted about a case, review some preliminary information, give a brief response, and then never hear anything else because the attorney chose someone else.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Do that enough times and it can become a real time suck. That’s one reason why, so far, I’ve preferred building direct relationships with attorneys.

And once you do get a case, my early impression is that the best marketing strategy is probably incredibly simple: Do a good job.

Be responsive. Be timely. You also need to be thorough without writing a 47-page treatise when three pages will do. Answer the questions being asked. Be easy to work with.

And most importantly, be honest. If your opinion isn’t what the attorney wants to hear, that’s still your opinion. The entire value of being an expert witness comes from being objective.

Do those things consistently and, I suspect, repeat business and referrals will follow.

There is one major part of expert witness work that I still haven’t experienced: Testifying.

I haven’t been deposed or testified at trial yet. So that’s an obvious blind spot in everything I’m saying here.

From talking to more experienced physician experts, my understanding is that most cases don’t ultimately involve courtroom testimony. A lot of the work is record review, conversations with attorneys, and written reports. Still, testimony is different. Being questioned by an opposing attorney while defending your opinions is not something we routinely do in clinical medicine.

When I eventually have that experience, I’ll write about it.

Physician expert witness work isn’t passive income. It’s scalable but requires effort, much in the same way that other physician side income streams can potentially require. And it isn’t something where you send a few emails and immediately have an overflowing pipeline of cases.

But it does something that I think is incredibly valuable for physicians.

It takes expertise that we already spent years, really decades, developing and gives us another way to use it. And unexpectedly, I think it has already made me a better physician.

Reading cases retrospectively makes you think differently about documentation. It makes you think about how clinical decisions will look when someone reviews the chart a year later without any of the context you had in the moment. I’ve already found myself bringing some of those lessons back into my own practice.

A handful of hours of expert witness work can generate income comparable to working an extra clinical shift. Except I can do those hours before my kids wake up, at a practice, or whenever else they fit into my life.

And that gets back to the whole reason I’m pursuing financial freedom as a physician in the first place.

The goal isn’t just more money. It’s more control over my time. Three months in, expert witness work seems like a pretty good way to create a little more of both.
